newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - WEEK AHEAD - Australian imports feature of week.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - WEEK AHEAD - Australian imports feature of week.

text.p: The week ahead is looking quiet for Australian financial markets, with Monday morning's import release the major data of the week.
The rest of the week will be spent watching the U.S., keeping an eye on Canberra in case the mid-year review of the budget is released, and preparing for December quarter CPI data due on January 29.
Imports have risen in each of the last four months, and a flat result is expected for December.

Following on the imports release, economists will be making their last projections for the monthly current account deficit -- the December current account is to be the last monthly current account deficit, replaced by a quarterly current account report and a monthly balance of trade and services report.
BONDS (Fri 10-yr cash 7.43 pct, 3-yr cash 6.55)
A dearth of local data, unless the mid-year review is released, means bonds are expected to follow the U.S. market this week, with Greenspan's Senate appearance the major event.
At the end of floor trading last week, bonds were sitting just under resistance in the low to mid 92.50s for the 10-year contract and the mid 93.50's for the three year contract.

The local interest rate picture had been confused by the news on Thursday that a new sampling method may have been producing lower employment estimates than the previous survey method, and so may have been presenting an artificially weak picture of the labour market.
Sentiment still favoured a local rate cut, which should keep the short end well supported, but the expected timing had been pushed out, which may see March bill futures weaken.
Bankers Trust interest rate strategist Rory Robertson said he had revised his probability of another cut down to 55/60 percent from 75/80 percent before the labour force data.

"The excellent inflation and positive wages outlook will probably be enough to eventually generate another rate cut reward, but there now seems to be less need to ease again to boost the economy," he said.
"Importantly, the recent news pushes out the likely timing of the next move, from Februaru/March to March, April or even May," Robertson said.
But the main hurdle for markets will be Greenspan's appearance before Senate Budget committee to talk about the U.S. economy.

With the U.S. market nervous about the prospect of higher rates, traders said any warnings from Greenspan on the dangers of inflation are likely to see Treasuries sold across the curve, and local bonds follow, particularly at the long end.
"Given recent uncertainty over the outlook for U.S. monetary policy, his comments have the potential to make or break an already jittery bond market," Commonwealth Bank economist Tim Moloney said.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri close US$0.7790, NY US$0.7795)

The Australian dollar faces another tough week as the market continues to fret over the risk of another cut in domestic interest rates, a danger which has already caused Japanese demand for A$ samurai bonds to dry up.

The currency had found a surprising depth of support at the 5-1/2 month low of US$0.7738, partly thanks to enthusiastic bids from a well known Asian bank, which forced a short market to square up by the end of last week.

Fresh weakness in the mark and yen had also provided a cushion for the currency and that trend looked set to continue with interest rates in Japan and Germany expected to remain low or even fall further.
The dollar will be haunted, however, by the risk of another Reserve Bank easing which much of the market is betting on for the next board meeting on February 4.
That belief will tend to keep the dollar bottled below US$0.7840 resistance, dealers said, and could well see it re-test US$0.7740 as time ticks down toward the board meeting.
AUSTRALIAN SHARES (Friday All Ords 2435.5, down 0.8)

With the market having comfortably consolidated at higher levels on the back of firm base metals prices and an upbeat Wall Street, the focus turns back to local corporate events of enough import to move the market.
"National Australia Bank releases quarterly results and has its annual meeting, as does Westpac, and we will be looking to those," said a Sydney-based funds manager.
Australia's largest bank, National Australia Bank, is expected to release its first quarter results, while its annual meeting is in Melbourne on Thursday. Westpac meets in Sydney on Monday.
While the miners saw their recent rally curtailed as base metals prices took a breather, any show of strength will see the resource leaders resume their uptrend.
Combined with continuing support for the banks, possibly dependent on this week's meetings and results, further gains were seen possible.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
